## Introduction

This tutorial covers [Chapter 8: Linear regression with multiple predictors](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/model-mlr.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You will learn how a regression model uses indicator and categorical predictors, how to fit and read a model with many predictors at once, and how to choose among models with adjusted R-squared, using backward elimination and forward selection.

### Exercise 1

You should be doing this tutorial in a repo named `linear-regression-with-multiple-predictors`. If you are not, create one and then connect to it.

```bash

```

Open `analysis.html` with Live Server (right-click it in the Explorer → **Open with Live Server**) and keep the tab open. It refreshes on every render. Going forward, we will just tell you to "Render" when we want you to take these steps.

Create a `.gitignore` with `analysis_files` followed by a blank line. Commit and push. Use AI however you like.


###

Multiple regression extends single predictor variable regression to the case that still has one response but many predictors. Our one response is the interest rate on a loan, and our predictors describe the loan and the borrower.

## Categorical and many predictors

The outcome variable we would like to better understand is the interest rate assigned to the loan. We build the chapter's `loans` data, then fit models with an indicator predictor, a categorical predictor, and finally every predictor at once.

### Exercise 9

Replace the code in that chunk so that it fits a linear model of `interest_rate` with `bankruptcy` as the only predictor, and shows just the term and the estimate for each coefficient, to two decimal places. Render.

```{r}
#| label: categorical-and-many-predictors-9
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: categorical-and-many-predictors-9-test
#| echo: true
lm(interest_rate ~ bankruptcy, data = loans) |>
  tidy() |>
  select(term, estimate) |>
  mutate(estimate = num(estimate, digits = 2))
```

###

The intercept, 12.34, is the mean rate without a bankruptcy, and 12.34 + 0.74 is the mean with one. A slope of 0.74 means that the model predicts a 0.74% higher interest rate for those borrowers with a bankruptcy in their record.

### Exercise 12

Replace the code in that chunk so that it fits a linear model of `interest_rate` using every other variable in `loans` as a predictor, and shows just the term and the estimate for each coefficient, to two decimal places. Render.

```{r}
#| label: categorical-and-many-predictors-12

```

```{r}
#| label: categorical-and-many-predictors-12-test
#| echo: true
lm(interest_rate ~ ., data = loans) |>
  tidy() |>
  select(term, estimate) |>
  mutate(estimate = num(estimate, digits = 2))
```

###

Seven predictors produce nine slopes, because a categorical predictor with $p$ different levels will be represented by $p - 1$ terms in a multiple regression model. The `bankruptcy` slope fell from 0.74 to 0.39 because the one-predictor model was constructed in a vacuum and did not consider the full context of everything that is considered when an interest rate is decided.

## Adjusted R-squared and model selection

One challenge to working with multiple variables is that it is sometimes difficult to know which variables are most important to include in the model. This section chooses among models with adjusted R-squared, using backward elimination and forward selection.

### Exercise 1

Start a new chunk that fits the full model of `interest_rate` on every other variable in `loans` and shows its R-squared and adjusted R-squared, to four decimal places. Render.

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-r-squared-and-model-selection-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-r-squared-and-model-selection-1-test
#| echo: true
lm(interest_rate ~ ., data = loans) |>
  glance() |>
  select(r.squared, adj.r.squared) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) num(x, digits = 4)))
```

###

The full model explains about 26% of the variability in interest rates, and the adjusted value, 0.2597, is slightly smaller. The regular $R^2$ is a biased estimate of the amount of variability explained by the model when applied to model with more than one predictor.

### Exercise 2

Replace the code in that chunk so that it calculates both numbers by hand from the full model's residuals and the outcomes of the loans it used: the variance of the residuals, the variance of `interest_rate`, the number of loans `n`, R-squared, and adjusted R-squared with `k = 9` predictors, all to four decimal places. Render.

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-r-squared-and-model-selection-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-r-squared-and-model-selection-2-test
#| echo: true
lm(interest_rate ~ ., data = loans) |>
  augment() |>
  summarize(var_resid = var(.resid),
            var_outcome = var(interest_rate),
            n = n()) |>
  mutate(r_squared = 1 - var_resid / var_outcome,
         adj_r_squared = 1 - var_resid / var_outcome * (n - 1) / (n - 9 - 1)) |>
  mutate(across(-n, \(x) num(x, digits = 4)))
```

###

The adjusted version multiplies the variance ratio by $(n - 1) / (n - k - 1)$. Because $k$ is never negative, the adjusted $R^2$ will be smaller -- often times just a little smaller -- than the unadjusted $R^2$.

### Exercise 3

Replace the code in that chunk so that it adds a column of pure random noise to `loans`, fits the full model with that noise as one more predictor, and shows R-squared and adjusted R-squared to five decimal places. Set the random seed to 8 first. Render.

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-r-squared-and-model-selection-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-r-squared-and-model-selection-3-test
#| echo: true
set.seed(8)
loans |>
  mutate(noise = rnorm(n())) |>
  lm(interest_rate ~ ., data = _) |>
  glance() |>
  select(r.squared, adj.r.squared) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) num(x, digits = 5)))
```

###

Noise nudged R-squared up, from 0.26036 to 0.26040, while adjusted R-squared fell, from 0.25969 to 0.25966. If we were to make predictions for *new data* using our current model, we would find that the unadjusted $R^2$ would tend to be slightly overly optimistic, while the adjusted $R^2$ formula helps correct this bias.

### Exercise 4

Replace the code in that chunk so that, for each of the seven predictors in turn, it fits the full model without that one predictor and records its adjusted R-squared. Show the results in a table sorted from highest to lowest, with adjusted R-squared to four decimal places. Render.

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-r-squared-and-model-selection-4
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-r-squared-and-model-selection-4-test
#| echo: true
tibble(dropped = c("verified_income", "debt_to_income", "credit_util",
                   "bankruptcy", "term", "credit_checks", "issue_month")) |>
  mutate(adj_r_squared = map_dbl(dropped, \(x) {
    lm(interest_rate ~ ., data = select(loans, -all_of(x))) |>
      glance() |>
      pull(adj.r.squared)
  })) |>
  arrange(desc(adj_r_squared)) |>
  mutate(adj_r_squared = num(adj_r_squared, digits = 4))
```

###

This is the first step of *backward elimination*, which starts with the full model -- the model that includes all potential predictor variables. Dropping `issue_month` raises adjusted R-squared from 0.2597 to 0.2598, so it goes, while dropping `term` costs the most.

### Exercise 5

Replace the code in that chunk so that it repeats the step with `issue_month` already removed: for each of the six remaining predictors, drop it as well and record the adjusted R-squared. Render.

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-r-squared-and-model-selection-5
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-r-squared-and-model-selection-5-test
#| echo: true
tibble(dropped = c("verified_income", "debt_to_income", "credit_util",
                   "bankruptcy", "term", "credit_checks")) |>
  mutate(adj_r_squared = map_dbl(dropped, \(x) {
    lm(interest_rate ~ ., data = select(loans, -issue_month, -all_of(x))) |>
      glance() |>
      pull(adj.r.squared)
  })) |>
  arrange(desc(adj_r_squared)) |>
  mutate(adj_r_squared = num(adj_r_squared, digits = 4))
```

###

No row beats the new baseline of 0.2598, so backward elimination stops. Predictors are eliminated one-at-a-time from the model until we cannot improve the model any further.

### Exercise 6

Replace the code in that chunk with the model that backward elimination chose, every predictor except `issue_month`, showing just the term and the estimate for each coefficient, to two decimal places. Render.

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-r-squared-and-model-selection-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-r-squared-and-model-selection-6-test
#| echo: true
lm(interest_rate ~ . - issue_month, data = loans) |>
  tidy() |>
  select(term, estimate) |>
  mutate(estimate = num(estimate, digits = 2))
```

###

The remaining estimates barely moved from the full model's, because `issue_month` explained almost nothing. It's common (and hip, at least in the statistical world) to refer to models that have undergone such predictor pruning as *parsimonious*.

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-r-squared-and-model-selection-7-test
#| echo: true
tibble(added = c("verified_income", "debt_to_income", "credit_util",
                 "bankruptcy", "term", "credit_checks", "issue_month")) |>
  mutate(adj_r_squared = map_dbl(added, \(x) {
    lm(interest_rate ~ ., data = select(loans, interest_rate, all_of(x))) |>
      glance() |>
      pull(adj.r.squared)
  })) |>
  arrange(desc(adj_r_squared)) |>
  mutate(adj_r_squared = num(adj_r_squared, digits = 5))
```

###

*Forward selection* adds `term` first, and `issue_month` comes out below zero, worse than a baseline model that has no predictors, which always has $R_{adj}^2 = 0$. The chapter's list swaps `issue_month` and `credit_checks`.

`credit_util` wins, lifting adjusted R-squared from 0.12855 to 0.20085. Continuing the same way adds `verified_income`, `credit_checks`, `debt_to_income`, and `bankruptcy`, then stops before `issue_month`: the same model backward elimination found.

### Exercise 9

Replace the code in that chunk with a table of the forward-selection path. Add the predictors one at a time in the order term, credit_util, verified_income, credit_checks, debt_to_income, bankruptcy, issue_month, and record the adjusted R-squared of the model after each addition, to four decimal places. Render.

```{r}

```

###

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-r-squared-and-model-selection-9-test
#| echo: true
predictors <- c("term", "credit_util", "verified_income", "credit_checks",
                "debt_to_income", "bankruptcy", "issue_month")

tibble(step = 1:7, added = predictors) |>
  mutate(adj_r_squared = map_dbl(step, \(i) {
    lm(interest_rate ~ ., data = select(loans, interest_rate, all_of(predictors[1:i]))) |>
      glance() |>
      pull(adj.r.squared)
  })) |>
  mutate(adj_r_squared = num(adj_r_squared, digits = 4))
```

###

The first two predictors lift adjusted R-squared to 0.20, and the next four add only about 0.06 together. Backward elimination and forward selection can arrive at different final models, because the decision for whether to include a given predictor or not depends on the other predictors that are already in the model.

```{r}
                "debt_to_income", "bankruptcy", "issue_month")

tibble(step = 1:7, added = predictors) |>
  mutate(adj_r_squared = map_dbl(step, \(i) {
```

```{r}
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.1, 0.3)) +

       subtitle = "Term and credit utilization do most of the work; adding issue month lowers adjusted R-squared",

       y = "Adjusted R-squared",
       caption = "Up to 10,000 Lending Club loans, January to March 2018; openintro package")
```

###

It is highly advised that *before* you begin the model selection process, you decide what a "meaningful" difference in adjusted $R^2$ is for the context of your data. With a threshold of even 0.01, forward selection would have stopped after `credit_checks`, at four predictors instead of six.

## Summary

This tutorial covered [Chapter 8: Linear regression with multiple predictors](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/model-mlr.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You have learned how a regression model uses indicator and categorical predictors, how to fit and read a model with many predictors at once, and how to choose among models with adjusted R-squared, using backward elimination and forward selection.

With real data, there is often a need to describe how multiple variables can be modeled together. In this tutorial, we have presented one approach using multiple linear regression. Each coefficient represents how the model predicts the outcome might change with one unit increase of that predictor *given* the rest of the predictor variables in the model. Working with and interpreting multivariable models can be tricky, especially when the predictor variables show multicollinearity. There is often no perfect or "right" final model, however, using the adjusted $R^2$ value is one way to identify important predictor variables for a final regression model. In later tutorials we will generalize multiple linear regression models to a larger population of interest from which the dataset was sampled.

For what these same models say about the population the loans came from, read [Chapter 25: Inference for regression with multiple predictors](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/inf-model-mlr.html), which returns to the `loans` data. For more on turning models into tidy tables, see the **broom** [introduction](https://broom.tidymodels.org/articles/broom.html).

Many sentences in this tutorial come from the chapter, used under the book's [CC BY-SA 3.0 license](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/).

````{verbatim}
loans <- loans_full_schema |>
  mutate(credit_util = total_credit_utilized / total_credit_limit,
         bankruptcy = as.factor(if_else(public_record_bankrupt == 0, 0, 1)),
         verified_income = droplevels(verified_income)) |>
  rename(credit_checks = inquiries_last_12m) |>
  select(interest_rate, verified_income, debt_to_income, credit_util,
         bankruptcy, term, credit_checks, issue_month)

summary(loans)
```

```{r}
````
